records.question: What must a data protection impact assessment contain at a minimum?
records.answer: Based on **GDPR Article 35**, specifically paragraph 7(c) [found in source [1]] and paragraphs 4-6 of the provided text, a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) must contain specific elements. The assessment requires at least: (a) a systematic description of the envisaged processing operations and their purposes; (b) an assessment of the necessity and proportionality of those operations in relation to the stated purposes [1][4]; (c) an evaluation of risks to data subjects' rights and freedoms, including new technologies or profiling where applicable [1][3]; and (d) measures envisaged to address identified risks, such as safeguards and security mechanisms [1]. records.answer: An organization is obliged to designate a data protection officer in three specific situations outlined in GDPR Article 37 [4]. records.question: Can a bank reject my loan application purely through an algorithm without any human involvement?
records.answer: Under GDPR Article 22, you have the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling, which produces legal effects concerning you [3]. This means a bank cannot legally make your loan approval or rejection decision purely through an algorithm without any human involvement. The law requires that suitable measures safeguarding your rights are implemented in such cases, specifically the right to obtain human intervention and contest the decision [3]. While DPDP Act Section 17 allows processing for ascertaining financial information regarding defaults, it does not explicitly override the general prohibition against sole automated decisions affecting legal status like loan approval under GDPR principles which often inform similar data protection frameworks globally [2][3]. If such a purely algorithmic rejection occurs without human review, you may have grounds to contest that specific decision based on your rights under Article 22 of GDPR or analogous provisions in the DPDP Act regarding automated processing safeguards.

records.question: Can I get my data from one online service in a machine-readable format and move it to a competitor?

records.answer: Under GDPR Article 20, you have the right to receive your personal data in a structured, commonly used, and machine-readable format [1]. Additionally, exercising these rights must not adversely affect the rights and freedoms of others [1][4]. records.question: What must a contract between a controller and a processor stipulate?

retrieved.section_title: Processing under the authority of the controller or processor

records.answer: Under GDPR Article 28(3), a contract or other legal act between a controller and a processor must set out specific details including the subject-matter, duration, nature, purpose of processing, type of personal data, categories of data subjects, and the obligations and rights of both parties. The same provision further requires that the processor stipulate how it shall process only on documented instructions from the controller [1][3]. Additionally, if a code of conduct or certification is used to demonstrate sufficient guarantees, adherence to such mechanisms may be referenced within these contractual arrangements as an element satisfying data protection obligations [2][5]. The contract must also explicitly state that any engagement by the processor of another processor requires prior written authorization from the controller and imposes similar data protection obligations on sub-processors via separate contracts or legal acts [3][4]. Finally, all such agreements between controllers and processors are required to be in writing, which may include electronic form [9].

records.question: Under what condition can personal data be sent to a non-EU country without any specific authorisation?

retrieved.section_title: Transfers on the basis of an adequacy decision

records.answer: Personal data may be transferred to a third country or international organisation without requiring specific authorization if that entity has been found to ensure an adequate level of protection by the Commission, as established under GDPR Article 45(1) [1]. Alternatively, such a transfer can occur on one of several derogations listed in GDPR Article 49(1), provided there is no adequacy decision or appropriate safeguards in place [2]. Another possibility exists if the data subject has explicitly consented to the proposed transfer after being informed of the associated risks under GDPR Article 49(1)(a) [2], though this does not constitute a general exemption from authorization requirements. Furthermore, transfers based on binding corporate rules adopted by the Commission or approved codes of conduct are permitted without specific authorisation under GDPR Article 46(2) [4]. Finally, any transfer must comply with the general principle that conditions laid down in Chapter V be met to ensure the level of protection is not undermined per GDPR Article 44 [5], and judgments from third countries requiring disclosure generally require a mutual legal assistance treaty unless other grounds apply under GDPR Article 48 [3].
